profiles.meeting_scenario: A 30-minute brainstorming meeting at a large SaaS company between the developer productivity team and an applied research engineer who recently synthesized findings from a systematic literature review on source code similarity and clone detection. The team is considering an internal prototype that could surface similar code during pull requests, identify duplicate implementations across the monorepo, and later support code recommendation use cases. The agenda is to generate candidate prototype directions, decide what a sensible first pilot would look like, and identify what evidence would be enough to screen ideas without committing to a full build. The expected outcome is a short list of 2-3 promising prototype concepts and a shared sense of the first experiment to run.

members.name: Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Monorepo tooling, static analysis infrastructure, build pipelines, developer workflow instrumentation
members.background: Lena has spent six years building internal code intelligence tools, including indexing services and a duplicate-code dashboard used by several backend teams; she is practical, delivery-oriented, and familiar with the company's Java-heavy service stack.
members.private_state: She wants the brainstorming to converge on something that can reuse existing parsing and indexing infrastructure and show visible value within one quarter, while avoiding a research-heavy evaluation setup that would delay implementation.
hidden_assumptions: "Support a language" mainly means the pipeline can parse, index, and compare files in that language well enough to expose an internal feature flag.
"Pilot on payments" naturally refers to the hand-written application code developers edit regularly, not tests, fixtures, generated clients, or vendored artifacts.
A "lightweight evaluation" is sufficient if it uses a small manually inspected internal sample and basic latency/usability checks to rank prototype ideas.
Public datasets from the literature review are useful external references, but they are optional until after an internal prototype direction is chosen.

members.name: Ravi Menon
members.expertise: Machine learning for code, empirical software engineering, clone detection literature, representation learning
members.background: Ravi recently joined from a research lab where he worked on code representation models and reproducible benchmarking, and he prepared the review summary that highlighted dataset gaps, hybrid methods, and limited language coverage in prior work.
members.private_state: He wants the discussion to preserve a path to a publishable and generalizable system rather than a narrowly internal heuristic, and he is concerned that an overly local pilot will bias the team toward the easiest infrastructure rather than the most robust idea.
hidden_assumptions: "Support a language" means the system handles normalization and explanation well enough that similarity results are credible and transferable across real use cases in that language.
"Pilot on payments" implies using the full repository slice that represents the corpus developers actually search over, including tests, generated code, and client stubs.
A "lightweight evaluation" still needs at least a minimal cross-family comparison of techniques, not just a few spot checks, so that screening decisions are defensible.
Because the prep material emphasized the eight publicly accessible datasets, those datasets are already the default shared starting point for early benchmarking.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the prototype should "support Java first" and later "add Python."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the existing parser/indexer can ingest Java and produce similarity candidates that are usable enough for an internal pilot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means Java results should already include language-aware normalization and interpretable matching behavior strong enough to count as substantive support rather than mere ingestion.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In software tooling meetings, "support" is a routine shorthand that often goes unexpanded; both are comfortable saying Java-first, so the phrase creates a false sense of precision while hiding different completeness thresholds.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the payments pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to "pilot on payments" or "use the payments service as the first slice."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the pilot corpus is the hand-written production code under the main payments service directories, excluding tests, generated protobuf/grpc clients, and fixtures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the pilot corpus includes the whole payments repository slice, including tests and generated code, because those files shape the real similarity distribution and challenge false positives.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants view their interpretation as the obvious default meaning of a service-level pilot, and neither expects the other to mentally enumerate repository boundaries during an early brainstorming discussion.

misalignment_points.topic: What qualifies as a lightweight evaluation
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both endorse doing a "lightweight evaluation" before choosing a prototype direction.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks lightweight means a fast internal screen: a few dozen sampled examples, manual inspection of obvious clone patterns, and a basic latency/usability check on one service.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks lightweight still means comparing at least one representative baseline from multiple technique families on a small but explicit benchmark mix before screening ideas.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are trying to avoid a heavy formal study, so "lightweight" sounds aligned and pragmatic; the disagreement is not over whether to evaluate, but over the silent threshold for what counts as enough evidence.

misalignment_points.topic: Status of the public datasets from the review
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to "the public datasets from the review" as part of the discussion setup.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes those datasets are background context and maybe a later sanity check, not an already-committed ingredient in the first experiment.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the team already accepts those datasets as the default benchmarking substrate because they were highlighted in the review memo and are the publicly accessible options.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The review memo made the datasets salient without explicitly assigning them a decision status, so each participant treats a different implication of the same prep material as already shared context.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to land on something we can ship a visible prototype for this quarter, ideally by leaning on the Java parser and indexing stack we already run. Ravi's review is useful, especially the parts about hybrid approaches and thin benchmarking coverage, but I don't want us to disappear into a long evaluation exercise before we even know whether developers will care.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. What I'd like to get out of this is a short list of realistic prototype directions for code similarity that are informed by your review, especially the gaps around limited datasets, the tradeoffs across clone-detection approaches, and the hybrid opportunities. If we leave with two or three candidate shapes and a sensible first experiment, that's a good use of the half hour.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this from collapsing into 'whatever the existing infra can do fastest.' If we say we support Java first, I want that to mean results are actually credible, normalized appropriately, and explainable enough to generalize. turns.inner_thought: A hybrid is the sweet spot if we define it pragmatically: start with token fingerprints and the infrastructure we already trust, get something useful in Java fast, then later expand the ingestion path to Python once the prototype proves out.
